opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core of it is that the models themselves have gotten remarkably capable, much faster than most enterprises have been able to absorb them. If you look at what a frontier model can do today in terms of reasoning, writing code, and working through a multi-step problem, there's a huge gap between that raw capability and the value that's actually being captured inside a typical company. That gap is the opportunity.

Part of the reason the gap exists is that a model on its own isn't a product. To do real work in an enterprise, you need the model connected to the company's data, its internal tools, and its permissions and access controls. You need it embedded in the workflows people already use. You need evaluation, so you know whether it's actually doing the job well, and you need some way of handling the cases where it fails. None of that comes for free with the model. It's systems engineering, and it's often very specific to the domain and the customer.

What I find exciting is that this is where a lot of the durable value is going to be built. The model providers will keep pushing capability forward, and I expect that to continue for a while. But each time the models get better, the set of tasks you can automate or augment gets bigger, and so the demand for people who know how to take that capability and turn it into something reliable inside a real organization actually grows. It's a bit like what happened with electricity or with the internet. The underlying technology arrives, and then there's a long period where the real economic impact comes from rebuilding processes around it.

There's also a reliability point that I think people underestimate. In a demo you can get something that works eighty percent of the time and it looks magical. In an enterprise, eighty percent often isn't usable. Getting from eighty to ninety-nine percent on a specific business process requires careful scaffolding around the model, with the right context, the right checks, and humans in the loop where it matters. That's hard and unglamorous work, but it's exactly what unlocks adoption.

So when I put all that together, I see very powerful general-purpose models, enterprises that know they need to use them but often don't know how, and a lot of hard, specific work in between. That's a pretty classic recipe for a big opportunity.

r001.rationale: The response says models need connections to company data, tools, and permissions to do enterprise work, but does not clearly state that the systems enable decisions informed by that internal context.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that training a separate model for each enterprise problem is not worthwhile for frontier AI labs.

r003.rationale: It discusses connecting models to enterprise context, but does not identify a shared enterprise problem involving moving context into models and outputs back out.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing people underestimate is how much of the value is actually downstream of the model. The models themselves are getting really good, and they're going to keep getting better. But when you drop one into a real enterprise, it's not like you get a drop-in employee. The model doesn't know anything about your company. It doesn't know your data, it doesn't know your processes, it doesn't know what "done" means for a given task. All of that context lives in the systems around it.

So the opportunity is in that gap. You have this incredibly capable raw intelligence on one side, and on the other side you have businesses with decades of accumulated process, data sitting in twenty different places, and workflows that were designed for humans. Somebody has to build the connective tissue: the retrieval, the tool access, the evaluation loops, the guardrails, the way you actually verify that the thing did what it was supposed to do. That's where most of the engineering effort ends up going, and honestly, that's where a lot of the differentiation ends up being too.

And I'd add one more thing. When I was at OpenAI, a lot of the conversation was about capabilities, like what can the model do in principle. But enterprises don't buy "in principle." They buy reliability. They need the thing to work 99 percent of the time, not 80 percent, and getting from 80 to 99 is almost entirely a systems problem rather than a model problem. That's a huge amount of work, and it's work that's going to be needed for every company, in every industry. So when I look at where the economic value is going to get created over the next several years, a big chunk of it is in building those systems.

r001.rationale: The response says enterprise context lives in surrounding systems and identifies retrieval and tool access as ways to connect that context to models.

r002.rationale: It does not say that frontier AI labs would find enterprise-specific model training not worthwhile.

r003.rationale: It describes shared connective systems for enterprise context, tool access, and verifying model outputs, and says this work is needed for every company and industry.

astra-6.text:
I think the model is only one piece of what an enterprise needs. To do useful work, it needs access to the right information, connections to the tools people already use, and a way to check whether it actually accomplished the task. You also need permissions and human review where the stakes warrant it.

There’s a lot of opportunity in building that surrounding system. You can take a workflow that involves people moving information between several applications and make it much easier to complete. The value comes from understanding that workflow and making the whole thing work reliably. As models get more capable, the range of workflows you can address gets larger.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss training a model for each enterprise or whether that is worthwhile for frontier AI labs.

r003.rationale: It describes workflows moving information between applications, but does not identify a shared enterprise problem of moving context into models and outputs back out.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a big gap between what a model can do in a demo and what an enterprise needs it to do reliably every day. The model might be able to answer a question or perform a task, but it needs access to the right data, the right tools, and the right permissions. You also need a way to evaluate whether it’s doing a good job and bring a person in when it gets stuck.

That creates a lot of room to build valuable systems around the models. If you understand a particular business workflow, you can take these general capabilities and turn them into something that actually gets work done. And as the models improve, those systems can take on more of the workflow. That’s why I see such a big opportunity there.
